The manipulation of time in the story is exceptionally well-balanced and serves the emotional arc of the narrative. The author uses **compression of time** at the beginning to quickly establish eight years of post-divorce routines and character dynamics in just a few paragraphs. Similarly, at the very end, months and years—covering the father's death in November, the funeral, and a year of exchanging letters with Eli—are compressed into a single paragraph. 

Conversely, the story slows down to focus on the seven-day cruise, pausing on specific days (the second day, the fourth night, the last night). During the climax at the White Party, the narrative **stretches time** during the three-to-four-minute slow dance between Josie and her father. By lingers on sensory details (the feel of his ribs, the sound of his heart, the circle of men) and their crucial dialogue, the author stretches this brief moment to maximize its emotional weight. Compressing the actual death at the end while stretching the dance honors the father's wish for how his story should be told—focusing on the life and love they shared rather than the tragedy of his passing.
